fixes.explanation: Peter goes in and sits down with the guards (Matthew 26:58). Sitting down next to them takes some nerve, friend. I'd have picked a seat by the exit, and then maybe a seat outside.

The two witnesses say Jesus claimed, "I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days." (Matthew 26:61) Many false witnesses came forward before them, but the council did not find the false testimony it was seeking (Matthew 26:60). Then these two come forward and declare it. It's the temple of God they bring up, friend.
The high priest asks, "Have You no answer?" (Matthew 26:62), and Jesus remains silent (Matthew 26:63). Nothing in the text has Him asking for His disciples. He just stays quiet.
Boasting is a word you might reach for, friend. But the high priest uses a different one. He tears his clothes and declares, "He has blasphemed!" (Matthew 26:65).

The high priest says, "Why do we need any more witnesses? Look, now you have heard the blasphemy." (Matthew 26:65) His point is that everyone in the room just heard Jesus' words with their own ears. Earlier the council had been seeking false testimony (Matthew 26:59). Now the high priest says they need no more witnesses.

The high priest asks, "What do you think?" and the council answers, "He deserves to die…" (Matthew 26:66) Back in verse 59, the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking false testimony in order to put Him to death. I think this is a heavy moment, friend.

The servant girl says, "You also were with Jesus the Galilean…" and Peter denies it before them all: "I do not know what you are talking about." (Matthew 26:69-70) I think this is a rough moment for Peter, since he followed Jesus all the way to this courtyard (Matthew 26:58). It's the first of the denials.
That line isn't in the text. Peter denies it before them all: "I do not know what you are talking about." (Matthew 26:70). He answers what she said directly, not with a travel story.

When Peter has gone out to the gateway, another servant girl sees him and tells the people there, "This man was with Jesus of Nazareth." (Matthew 26:71) Different girl, different spot. Peter changed locations, and the same claim followed him.

The text says it did happen. Peter goes out to the gateway, and another servant girl sees him and says to the people there, "This man was with Jesus of Nazareth." (Matthew 26:71) She's a second servant girl, not the first. Moving to a new spot didn't get Peter away from the claim.

Matthew 26:72 says Peter denied it again with an oath, saying, "I do not know the man!" That's the second denial, and it's stronger than the first one. In verse 70, he only said he didn't know what she meant. Now he's put an oath behind it.

The people standing nearby say, "Surely you are one of them, for your accent gives you away." (Matthew 26:73) The first two times it was servant girls, and this time it's a group standing close. That's more people talking to one man.

Matthew 26:74 says Peter began to curse and swear to them, and he says, "I do not know the man!" The first denial was words, the second an oath, and now this. And right then a rooster crowed. Peter is in deep, friend.

That's not what Matthew records. He says Peter began to curse and swear to them, and Peter says, "I do not know the man!" (Matthew 26:74). Nothing in the scene has him laughing. It's a heavy moment, friend.
Peter doesn't beg anybody to leave. Matthew says he began to curse and swear to them, and he says, "I do not know the man!" (Matthew 26:74). He's still pressing the denial.
Seven would be a lot of denials for Peter. The words Peter remembers are, "Before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times." (Matthew 26:75). Three is the number.
